Russia has expanded its nuclear cooperation with Brazil this year, increasing uranium processing contracts by 25 percent and becoming Brazil’s largest uranium supplier.



Moscow is moving beyond uranium exports toward deeper integration into Brazil’s nuclear fuel cycle, including conversion, enrichment, and potentially domestic uranium extraction.



Rosatom—Russia’s state-owned nuclear energy corporation—is seeking to broaden its presence in Brazil through critical mineral projects, small modular reactors, and potential participation in nuclear power plant construction.



Brazil’s plans to expand nuclear generating capacity present new opportunities for Moscow, but financing constraints and Brasília’s pursuit of technological sovereignty could limit Russia’s ambitions.

latest_rss.title: Central Asians Studying Chinese in Ever Greater Numbers
latest_rss.summary:
Executive Summary:




Ever more Central Asians are learning Chinese rather than Russian or English, convinced that Chinese is the foreign language of the future and that knowing it will help them find work with the growing number of Chinese firms and institutions in their countries.



Most Central Asians studying Chinese are doing so in Chinese-funded institutions, but a growing number are getting such instruction in local universities or from tutors, an indication that this Beijing effort at promoting its soft power in Central Asia is taking off.



At present, the numbers doing so are still relatively small compared to those studying Russian, the language of upward mobility in Soviet times, or English more recently; but they are growing rapidly and helping Beijing to cement its influence there.
